content: The Public Health Service (PHS) has issued detailed recommendations for managing healthcare personnel (HCP) who experience occupational exposure to blood or other body fluids potentially containing hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), or human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). These guidelines are designed to ensure timely and effective postexposure management to reduce the risk of infection transmission. For HBV postexposure management, it is recommended to initiate the hepatitis B vaccine series for any unvaccinated and susceptible individual who has been exposed. Postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) with hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) and/or the hepatitis B vaccine series should be considered based on the HBV surface antigen status of the source and the vaccination and immune response status of the exposed individual. Clinicians are provided with specific guidance to select the appropriate HBV PEP regimen. HBV PEP is highly effective, with studies showing that a combination of HBIG and the hepatitis B vaccine series can prevent infection in 85%-95% of cases when administered promptly. For HCV, PEP with immune globulin or antiviral agents is not recommended. Instead, the HCV status of both the source and the exposed individual should be determined. Follow-up testing for HCV is advised for HCP exposed to an HCV-positive source to monitor for potential infection development. Early identification of chronic HCV infection is critical for timely referral and evaluation of treatment options. For HIV, PEP typically involves a basic 4-week regimen of two antiretroviral drugs, such as zidovudine and lamivudine, for most exposures. For higher-risk exposures, a third drug may be added to the regimen. If the source virus is known or suspected to be resistant to one or more drugs, alternative agents should be selected based on the resistance profile. HIV PEP should be initiated as soon as possible, ideally within hours of exposure, to maximize its effectiveness in preventing systemic infection. Occupational exposures are considered urgent medical concerns, and immediate evaluation and management are essential. This includes the administration of HBIG, hepatitis B vaccine, and/or HIV PEP as appropriate. Delays in reporting or initiating treatment can reduce the effectiveness of prophylaxis. The PHS guidelines emphasize the importance of preventing occupational exposures through adherence to standard precautions and the use of safety devices. However, when exposures occur, these recommendations provide a comprehensive framework for managing the risk of infection and ensuring the safety of healthcare personnel.
